stated_availability: Single blanket statement covering both data and code: "The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252" (Data availability statement, p.10). In-text (p.2): "The entire R code (R Core Team, 2024) used for all the analysis and visualizations contained in this paper is at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252 ... All the figures, tables, and statistical test results presented here can be independently reproduced with the code and data in this compendium (Marwick, et al., 2018). The R code is released under the MIT license, the data as CC-0, and figures as CC-BY, to enable maximum re-use." Fig. 2 caption adds: "Further details about the model specifications and diagnostics are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252" (same DOI, split across a line wrap in the PDF).

F1.evidence: Data availability statement gives a resolvable DOI: 'The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252' (p.10).

F2.evidence: Unscoreable: the paper gives only a bare DOI link inline and in the availability statement, with no formatted citation (title/creators/keywords/description) to the Zenodo record itself and no description of its metadata fields; actual repository metadata richness is not evidenced in the text.

F3.evidence: The resource is a DOI (DataCite-registered via Zenodo/CERN); DOI registration structurally embeds the identifier in the record's own metadata as part of the minting process, and the paper consistently cites the identical DOI (10.5281/zenodo.14897252) for the resource itself, its data, and its documentation.

F4.evidence: Deposited on Zenodo, which the instrument's own F4 example lists as a qualifying searchable registry ('F4: ...(Zenodo, CRAN, DataCite)'); paper text also independently describes Zenodo as 'a non-profit generic research data repository hosted by CERN that accepts any file format and freely assigns all publicly available uploads a DOI' (p.8).

A1.evidence: Data-completeness coverage assessed as 'complete' (see data_completeness), so the A1 forced-zero rule does not apply. Statement: 'The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252' (p.10), retrievable via standard HTTPS download, no registration/paywall indicated, no ethical restriction stated.

A1_1.evidence: Zenodo is accessed via open, free HTTPS; no cost or proprietary client required to retrieve the DOI-linked record (platform property of the named repository, consistent with the paper's own description of Zenodo on p.8).

A1_2.evidence: Zenodo's HTTPS delivery protocol supports authentication/embargo where needed; the paper indicates no restriction is required here ('the data as CC-0', p.2), i.e. the protocol trivially satisfies this criterion since full open access was chosen and nothing blocks it.

A2.evidence: Zenodo/CERN's DOI persistence policy retains the metadata landing page even if files were later withdrawn -- a structural platform guarantee associated with the named DOI-issuing repository used here (p.8: 'CERN... freely assigns all publicly available uploads a DOI to make the files easily and uniquely citable').

I1.evidence: Unscoreable: the paper never states the file format(s) of the deposited data (e.g. CSV vs. R-specific binary .rds), so use of a formal, shared, non-proprietary representation cannot be evidenced from the text.

I2.evidence: No mention anywhere in the text of controlled vocabularies, ontologies, or FAIR-compliant vocabulary use for describing the dataset variables.

I3.evidence: No evidence that the deposited data's own metadata contains qualified/typed references (PIDs) to related resources (e.g. linking the dataset record to the article DOI or to related datasets); only the article text itself carries citation links.

R1.evidence: Dataset attributes are described in detail in Methods: 'I quantify the number of authors, length of article, relative title length, age of references, and diversity of references for a large sample of peer-reviewed journal articles' (p.2), with each variable further defined (e.g. Price index for recency, Shannon Index for diversity, p.2-3).

R1_1.evidence: 'the data as CC-0 ... to enable maximum re-use' (p.2) -- an explicit, clear, open data licence.

R1_2.evidence: Sampling/collection provenance is detailed: 'This sample was collected from Clarivate Web of Science database by first selecting the Web of Science category "Archaeology" and the Document type "article" (n = 28,871)... I analysed 9697 papers published during 1975-2025... included only articles published in the top-ranking 25 journals... excluded journals with less than 100 articles... resulting in 20 journals' (p.2); further modelling provenance pointer: 'Further details about the model specifications and diagnostics are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252' (Fig. 2 caption, p.4).

R1_3.evidence: Variable construction explicitly follows established bibliometric/scientometric community methods, e.g. following Fanelli and Glänzel (2013) and using recognised indices (Price index for recency, Shannon Index for diversity of references), situating the dataset within domain-standard bibliometric practice (p.2-3).

F1.evidence: Same DOI covers the code: 'The entire R code (R Core Team, 2024) used for all the analysis and visualizations contained in this paper is at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252' (p.2).

F2.evidence: Unscoreable: no formatted citation or description of the Zenodo record's own structured metadata (title/creators/keywords/description) is given in the paper text -- only a bare inline DOI link.

F3.evidence: DOI-registered Zenodo deposit; DataCite DOI minting structurally embeds the identifier within the record's own metadata, and the paper repeatedly and consistently cites the same DOI (10.5281/zenodo.14897252) to reference the code.

F4.evidence: Code is hosted on Zenodo, explicitly named as a qualifying registry example in the instrument's own F4 criterion; paper independently describes Zenodo as a CERN-hosted repository that 'freely assigns all publicly available uploads a DOI to make the files easily and uniquely citable' (p.8).

A1.evidence: 'All the figures, tables, and statistical test results presented here can be independently reproduced with the code and data in this compendium' (p.2) -- an explicit completeness claim for the code, retrievable via the same open Zenodo DOI.

A1_1.evidence: Retrieved via open, free HTTPS from Zenodo, no cost or restricted client required (platform property of the named repository, p.8).

A1_2.evidence: Zenodo's protocol supports authentication/embargo where required; code stated as fully open under MIT licence with no restriction invoked (p.2), so the criterion is satisfied by the protocol's inherent capability.

A2.evidence: Same Zenodo/CERN DOI-persistence guarantee applies to the code deposit as to the data deposit (p.8 description of Zenodo's DOI assignment and citability).

I1.evidence: Code is explicitly R: 'The entire R code (R Core Team, 2024) used for all the analysis and visualizations...' (p.2) -- R is a formal, open-source, widely documented, shared language/format (plain-text .R scripts), directly evidenced in text (also the dominant reproducibility-review software per Fig. 5A: 'R, followed by Python').

I2.evidence: No evidence of controlled vocabularies or standardised code-metadata schemas (e.g. CodeMeta) being used to describe the code or its dependencies.

I3.evidence: No textual evidence that the code repository's own metadata contains qualified/typed PID references to other resources (e.g. linked package DOIs, related-identifier links to the article).

R1.evidence: Code's purpose and scope are richly described: it reproduces 'all the figures, tables, and statistical test results' (p.2), with specific statistical methods detailed (Bayesian Generalized Additive Models, Zero-One Inflated Beta, Negative Binomial and Gaussian families, PCA, Borda Count ranking -- p.4-5) and a pointer to further model-specification documentation at the same DOI (Fig. 2 caption).

R1_1.evidence: 'The R code is released under the MIT license' (p.2) -- explicit, clear, permissive open-source licence.

R1_2.evidence: Detailed methodological/computational provenance given in-text (specific model families, link functions, software versions cited: 'R Core Team, 2024'), plus 'Further details about the model specifications and diagnostics are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14897252' (Fig. 2 caption, p.4).

R1_3.evidence: R is identified in the paper's own reproducibility-review data as the dominant language used by archaeologists (Fig. 5A), and the author explicitly aligns with community-recommended reproducible-compendium practice, citing his own prior methodological papers on packaging reproducible R-based research (Marwick, 2017; Marwick et al., 2018, cited p.2 and reference list) as the basis for this release.

barriers: Underlying raw Web of Science corpus (n=28,871 records queried, narrowed to 9,697 analysed) originates from a proprietary/subscription database (Clarivate Web of Science); the paper does not clarify whether raw WoS records or only the author's derived/computed bibliometric variables are redistributed in the Zenodo deposit -- treated as a potential but unstated/unconfirmed barrier, not counted against coverage given the explicit blanket availability statement.

Fanelli and Glänzel (2013) comparison values (overlaid reference boxplots in Fig. 1) are an upstream source from a separate publication rather than data hosted in this paper's own repository; however that source (PLoS One 8, e66938) is itself a fully open-access journal, so classified Tier 2 (accessible with some effort) rather than a blocking barrier.
